Optimism in older adults is associated with better health behaviors, more effective stress management, and stronger social connections, all of which contribute to increased longevity. Optimistic individuals are more likely to engage in preventive health behaviors—such as regular physical activity, adherence to medical advice, balanced nutrition, and avoidance of smoking or excessive alcohol use. These behaviors reduce the risk of chronic conditions common in later life, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers, thereby supporting a longer lifespan.  

From a psychological and physiological perspective, optimism influences how older adults respond to stress. Optimistic people tend to interpret stressors as manageable and temporary, which leads to lower and shorter-lived activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system. As a result, they generally exhibit lower chronic levels of stress hormones such as cortisol and catecholamines. Lower chronic stress is linked to reduced systemic inflammation, better immune function, healthier blood pressure regulation, and improved metabolic control—all factors that promote healthier aging and longevity.  

Optimism also supports better emotional well‑being, including lower rates of depression and anxiety. Good mental health can, in turn, improve sleep quality, pain tolerance, and motivation to maintain social and physical activity. Socially, optimistic older adults tend to maintain and build supportive relationships. Strong social networks provide emotional support, practical assistance, and a sense of purpose, and have been consistently linked to reduced mortality risk.  

In contrast, a pessimistic outlook can negatively affect health outcomes and shorten lifespan through several mechanisms. Pessimistic individuals are more likely to expect poor outcomes from efforts to improve health, which can reduce motivation to exercise, follow medical regimens, or seek timely medical care. This can lead to poorer control of chronic illnesses, more complications, and higher hospitalization rates.  

Pessimism also tends to amplify perceived stress: events are more likely to be interpreted as threatening, permanent, and uncontrollable. This can lead to more frequent and prolonged activation of stress-response systems, with elevated cortisol, increased blood pressure, and persistent low‑grade inflammation. Over time, these physiological changes increase the risk of atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, immune dysregulation, and neurodegeneration, all of which can shorten life expectancy.  

Furthermore, pessimism is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety in older adults. These conditions are associated with poorer self-care, social withdrawal, reduced physical activity, and in severe cases, increased risk of self-harm. Depression also has direct physiological correlates, including changes in inflammatory markers and autonomic balance, which are independently associated with higher mortality.  

In summary, optimism in older adults promotes healthier behaviors, more adaptive stress responses, and stronger social connections, all of which improve health outcomes and extend lifespan. Pessimistic outlooks, by contrast, can undermine motivation for self-care, heighten stress and its physiological consequences, and contribute to mental health problems, thereby negatively influencing both health status and longevity.

Energy expenditure varies significantly among human organs, reflecting differences in metabolic activity, cellular composition, and functional demands. When examined per unit of body mass, organs such as the brain, heart, kidneys, and liver have very high energy expenditure, while the intestines (particularly the large intestine) have comparatively low energy expenditure per unit mass.  

The brain, although it represents only a small percentage of total body weight, consumes a disproportionately large share of resting energy—primarily to maintain ion gradients, support synaptic transmission, and preserve cellular integrity. The heart also has high energy needs because it contracts continuously throughout life, requiring constant ATP production to sustain mechanical work and maintain ionic homeostasis in cardiac muscle cells. Similarly, the kidneys expend substantial energy for active transport processes involved in filtration, reabsorption, and secretion, which are necessary for regulating fluid, electrolyte, and acid–base balance. The liver is a major metabolic hub, responsible for gluconeogenesis, glycogen storage and breakdown, lipid and protein metabolism, and detoxification; this extensive biochemical activity leads to a high rate of ATP consumption per gram of tissue.  

In contrast, the intestines have lower energy expenditure per unit of body mass at rest. Several factors explain this. First, much of the intestinal tissue, especially in the large intestine, is structural and supportive (connective tissue, smooth muscle layers, and mucosa) rather than continuously engaged in high-intensity biochemical processing. Although the intestines do perform active transport for nutrient absorption and support peristaltic motion, these activities are intermittent and often elevated primarily during and shortly after meals. During fasting or rest, the metabolic demands of the intestines decrease significantly relative to organs that must function at high intensity continuously, such as the brain and heart.  

Second, some of the work of digestion and fermentation, particularly in the large intestine, is carried out by the gut microbiota. While these microorganisms are metabolically active, the energy they consume is not fully counted as the host’s own cellular energy expenditure per gram of host tissue. Additionally, the intestines can rely to some extent on locally produced or absorbed substrates (such as short-chain fatty acids in the colon) that provide fuel without requiring as much systemic energy redistribution.  

Third, the functional role of the intestines is more episodic: they alternate between periods of heightened activity (during digestion and absorption) and relatively quiescent periods. When averaged over time, this leads to a lower mean energy expenditure per unit mass than organs that lack such low-activity phases. Smooth muscle contractions in the gut are also generally less energy-demanding than the continuous, forceful contractions of cardiac muscle, and the enteric nervous system, while complex, operates with lower overall energy consumption than the central nervous system.  

In summary, while the intestines are essential for nutrient absorption and digestion, their energy demands per unit mass are lower than those of organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys. This is due to their more intermittent activity pattern, a higher proportion of relatively low-metabolic-rate tissue, partial reliance on microbial metabolism, and less continuous high-output mechanical or biochemical work.

Similarly, the kidneys expend substantial energy for active transport processes involved in filtration, reabsorption, and secretion, which are necessary for regulating fluid, electrolyte, and acid–base balance. The liver is a major metabolic hub, responsible for gluconeogenesis, glycogen storage and breakdown, lipid and protein metabolism, and detoxification; this extensive biochemical activity leads to a high rate of ATP consumption per gram of tissue.  

In contrast, the intestines have lower energy expenditure per unit of body mass at rest. Several factors explain this. First, much of the intestinal tissue, especially in the large intestine, is structural and supportive (connective tissue, smooth muscle layers, and mucosa) rather than continuously engaged in high-intensity biochemical processing. Although the intestines do perform active transport for nutrient absorption and support peristaltic motion, these activities are intermittent and often elevated primarily during and shortly after meals. During fasting or rest, the metabolic demands of the intestines decrease significantly relative to organs that must function at high intensity continuously, such as the brain and heart.  

Second, some of the work of digestion and fermentation, particularly in the large intestine, is carried out by the gut microbiota. While these microorganisms are metabolically active, the energy they consume is not fully counted as the host’s own cellular energy expenditure per gram of host tissue. Additionally, the intestines can rely to some extent on locally produced or absorbed substrates (such as short-chain fatty acids in the colon) that provide fuel without requiring as much systemic energy redistribution.  

Third, the functional role of the intestines is more episodic: they alternate between periods of heightened activity (during digestion and absorption) and relatively quiescent periods. When averaged over time, this leads to a lower mean energy expenditure per unit mass than organs that lack such low-activity phases. Smooth muscle contractions in the gut are also generally less energy-demanding than the continuous, forceful contractions of cardiac muscle, and the enteric nervous system, while complex, operates with lower overall energy consumption than the central nervous system.  

In summary, while the intestines are essential for nutrient absorption and digestion, their energy demands per unit mass are lower than those of organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys. This is due to their more intermittent activity pattern, a higher proportion of relatively low-metabolic-rate tissue, partial reliance on microbial metabolism, and less continuous high-output mechanical or biochemical work.

Optimism in older adults is associated with better health behaviors, more effective stress management, and stronger social connections, all of which contribute to increased longevity. Optimistic individuals are more likely to engage in preventive health behaviors—such as regular physical activity, adherence to medical advice, balanced nutrition, and avoidance of smoking or excessive alcohol use. These behaviors reduce the risk of chronic conditions common in later life, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers, thereby supporting a longer lifespan.  

From a psychological and physiological perspective, optimism influences how older adults respond to stress. Optimistic people tend to interpret stressors as manageable and temporary, which leads to lower and shorter-lived activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system. As a result, they generally exhibit lower chronic levels of stress hormones such as cortisol and catecholamines. Lower chronic stress is linked to reduced systemic inflammation, better immune function, healthier blood pressure regulation, and improved metabolic control—all factors that promote healthier aging and longevity.  

Optimism also supports better emotional well‑being, including lower rates of depression and anxiety. Good mental health can, in turn, improve sleep quality, pain tolerance, and motivation to maintain social and physical activity. Socially, optimistic older adults tend to maintain and build supportive relationships. Strong social networks provide emotional support, practical assistance, and a sense of purpose, and have been consistently linked to reduced mortality risk.  

In contrast, a pessimistic outlook can negatively affect health outcomes and shorten lifespan through several mechanisms. Pessimistic individuals are more likely to expect poor outcomes from efforts to improve health, which can reduce motivation to exercise, follow medical regimens, or seek timely medical care. This can lead to poorer control of chronic illnesses, more complications, and higher hospitalization rates.  

Pessimism also tends to amplify perceived stress: events are more likely to be interpreted as threatening, permanent, and uncontrollable. This can lead to more frequent and prolonged activation of stress-response systems, with elevated cortisol, increased blood pressure, and persistent low‑grade inflammation. Over time, these physiological changes increase the risk of atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, immune dysregulation, and neurodegeneration, all of which can shorten life expectancy.  

Furthermore, pessimism is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety in older adults. These conditions are associated with poorer self-care, social withdrawal, reduced physical activity, and in severe cases, increased risk of self-harm. Depression also has direct physiological correlates, including changes in inflammatory markers and autonomic balance, which are independently associated with higher mortality.  

In summary, optimism in older adults promotes healthier behaviors, more adaptive stress responses, and stronger social connections, all of which improve health outcomes and extend lifespan. Pessimistic outlooks, by contrast, can undermine motivation for self-care, heighten stress and its physiological consequences, and contribute to mental health problems, thereby negatively influencing both health status and longevity.
